claim: Accelerating discoveries of non-coding RNA (ncRNA) in myriad biological processes pose major challenges to structural and functional analysis.
source: Accelerating discoveries of non-coding RNA (ncRNA) in myriad biological processes pose major challenges to structural and functional analysis.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, drawing on established scientific knowledge about ncRNA research challenges.

claim: High-throughput methods have generally failed to determine ncRNA tertiary structures, even at the 1-nm resolution that enables visualization of how helices and functional motifs are positioned in three dimensions.
source: Despite progress in secondary structure modeling, high-throughput methods have generally failed to determine ncRNA tertiary structures, even at the 1-nm resolution that enables visualization of how helices and functional motifs are positioned in three dimensions.
evidence: This statement reflects the current limitations in the field based on established knowledge of existing methods.

claim: Integrating MOHCA-seq with mutate-and-map secondary structure inference guides Rosetta 3D modeling to consistent 1-nm accuracy for intricately folded ncRNAs with lengths up to 188 nucleotides.
source: We report that integrating a new method called MOHCA-seq (Multiplexed •OH Cleavage Analysis with paired-end sequencing) with mutate-and-map secondary structure inference guides Rosetta 3D modeling to consistent 1-nm accuracy for intricately folded ncRNAs with lengths up to 188 nucleotides, including a blind RNA-puzzle challenge, the lariat-capping ribozyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including modeling results for multiple RNAs shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The multidimensional chemical mapping (MCM) pipeline successfully modeled the lariat-capping ribozyme in a blind RNA-puzzle challenge.
source: We report that integrating a new method called MOHCA-seq (Multiplexed •OH Cleavage Analysis with paired-end sequencing) with mutate-and-map secondary structure inference guides Rosetta 3D modeling to consistent 1-nm accuracy for intricately folded ncRNAs with lengths up to 188 nucleotides, including a blind RNA-puzzle challenge, the lariat-capping ribozyme.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the blind prediction results for the lariat-capping ribozyme presented in the manuscript.

claim: MCM resolves unexpected tertiary proximities for cyclic-di-GMP, glycine, and adenosylcobalamin riboswitch aptamers without their ligands.
source: This multidimensional chemical mapping (MCM) pipeline resolves unexpected tertiary proximities for cyclic-di-GMP, glycine, and adenosylcobalamin riboswitch aptamers without their ligands and a loose structure for the recently discovered human HoxA9D internal ribosome entry site regulon.
evidence: This claim is supported by MOHCA-seq proximity maps and modeling data for ligand-free riboswitch states presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: MCM reveals a loose structure for the human HoxA9D internal ribosome entry site regulon.
source: This multidimensional chemical mapping (MCM) pipeline resolves unexpected tertiary proximities for cyclic-di-GMP, glycine, and adenosylcobalamin riboswitch aptamers without their ligands and a loose structure for the recently discovered human HoxA9D internal ribosome entry site regulon.
evidence: This is supported by experimental MOHCA-seq data and modeling results for the HoxA9 IRES domain shown in Figure 7.

claim: MCM offers a sequencing-based route to uncovering ncRNA 3D structure, applicable to functionally important but potentially heterogeneous states.
source: MCM offers a sequencing-based route to uncovering ncRNA 3D structure, applicable to functionally important but potentially heterogeneous states.
evidence: This is supported by the successful application of MCM to multiple RNA systems including heterogeneous ligand-free states, as demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Medium-sized non-coding RNA (ncRNA) domains in the 100- to 300-nucleotide size range have been discovered to form specific tertiary structures for sensing intra-cellular metabolites, regulating gene expression, and catalyzing precise splicing events.
source: In particular, medium-sized non-coding RNA (ncRNA) domains in the 100- to 300-nucleotide size range have been discovered to form specific tertiary structures for sensing intra-cellular metabolites, regulating gene expression, and catalyzing precise splicing events (Smith et al., 2009; Butler et al., 2011; Peselis & Serganov, 2012; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High-resolution structure determination techniques such as crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy are challenged by the large sizes, conformational heterogeneity, and multiple functional states of most biological ncRNA domains.
source: High-resolution structure determination techniques such as crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy are providing critical insights into ncRNA behavior but are challenged by the large sizes, conformational heterogeneity, and multiple functional states of most biological ncRNA domains (Weeks, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is a rich history of specialized biochemical interrogation, phylogenetic analysis, and manual model building to achieve global 3D structures of ncRNAs, including the first discovered ribozymes.
source: As an alternative methodology, there is a rich history of specialized biochemical interrogation, phylogenetic analysis, and manual model building to achieve global 3D structures of ncRNAs, including the first discovered ribozymes (Kim and Cech, 1987; Lehnert et al., 1996; Bergman et al., 2004; Kazantsev and Pace, 2006; Lipfert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to historical work in the field.

claim: Historical ncRNA models have reached nanometer accuracies, comparable to the spacing between adjacent nucleotides (6 Å) and significantly smaller than the diameter of an RNA helix (23 Å).
source: These models have reached nanometer accuracies, comparable to the spacing between adjacent nucleotides (6 Å) and significantly smaller than the diameter of an RNA helix (23 Å).
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about RNA structural dimensions and historical modeling achievements.

claim: The experimental and modeling methods underlying classic, medium-resolution approaches have not been fully automated or accelerated.
source: However, the experimental and modeling methods underlying these classic, medium-resolution approaches have not been fully automated or accelerated.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Recent advances have enhanced the throughput of chemical mapping analysis and the accuracy of ncRNA secondary structure determination.
source: Recent advances have enhanced the throughput of chemical mapping analysis and the accuracy of ncRNA secondary structure determination, with high accuracy achieved by 'two-dimensional' methods that integrate systematic mutagenesis with high-throughput mapping (mutate-and-map, or M2), analogous to multidimensional NMR spectroscopy but at nucleotide length scales (Kladwang et al., 2011a; Yoon et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2012; Mortimer et al., 2012; Karabiber et al., 2013; Seetin et al., 2014; Siegfried et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Barriers remain in 3D modeling, even at the modest 1-nanometer resolution required to visualize helix-level structures, to assess structural heterogeneity, or to make hypotheses for ligand-binding sites or tertiary interactions that can be experimentally tested.
source: However, barriers remain in 3D modeling, even at the modest 1-nanometer resolution required to visualize helix-level structures, to assess structural heterogeneity, or to make hypotheses for ligand-binding sites or tertiary interactions that can be experimentally tested.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field and the motivation for the present work.

claim: The state-of-the-art in ncRNA 3D structure modeling has been rigorously established by the 'RNA-puzzles' trials.
source: The state-of-the-art in ncRNA 3D structure modeling has been rigorously established by the 'RNA-puzzles' trials (Cruz et al., 2012; Miao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the RNA-puzzles literature.

claim: RNA-puzzles trials provide stringent tests of available computational methods by challenging modelers to predict structures of ncRNA sequences that have been crystallized but whose structures have not been publicly released.
source: These community-wide exercises provide stringent tests of available computational methods by challenging modelers to predict structures of ncRNA sequences that have been crystallized but whose structures have not been publicly released.
evidence: This describes the established methodology of RNA-puzzles based on cited literature.

claim: The dissemination of SHAPE, DMS, hydroxyl radical footprinting, and M2 measurements for recent RNA-puzzles has enabled consistent achievement of high-secondary structure prediction accuracies.
source: The dissemination of SHAPE, DMS, hydroxyl radical footprinting, and M2 measurements for recent RNA-puzzles has enabled our and other groups to consistently achieve high-secondary structure prediction accuracies.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' and others' participation in RNA-puzzles, as referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Computational integration of available data with the fragment assembly of RNA (FARNA) algorithm in Rosetta has led to tertiary structure models with accuracies of 1 nanometer or better (all-heavy-atom root-mean-squared-deviation, RMSD).
source: Furthermore, computational integration of available data with the fragment assembly of RNA (FARNA) algorithm in Rosetta (Cheng et al., 2015) has led to tertiary structure models with accuracies of 1 nanometer or better (all-heavy-atom root-mean-squared-deviation, RMSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is demonstrated by data in the current manuscript.

claim: Computational methods still generate alternative 3D structures consistent with the available data, and modelers have been unable to rank models with correct tertiary helical arrangements as top submissions.
source: Unfortunately, these computational methods still generate alternative 3D structures consistent with the available data. Out of the 5 to 10 different structures submitted by each participating modeling team for each puzzle, we and others have been unable to rank the models with correct tertiary helical arrangements as our top submissions, much less confidently assign accuracies to these models or select candidates for computationally expensive refinement.
evidence: This reflects the authors' experience in RNA-puzzles and the current limitations of modeling methods.

claim: The RNA-puzzles trials have exposed a critical need for rapid experimental methods to comprehensively determine nucleotide pairs that are not in direct atom–atom contact but are brought into nanometer-scale proximity by an ncRNA's tertiary structure.
source: While M2 efficiently infers Watson–Crick base pairs, the RNA-puzzles trials have exposed a critical need for rapid experimental methods to comprehensively determine nucleotide pairs that are not in direct atom–atom contact but are brought into nanometer-scale proximity by an ncRNA's tertiary structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the authors' experience with RNA-puzzles and the limitations of existing methods.

claim: The original MOHCA-gel protocol required specially synthesized 2′-NH2-2′-deoxy-α-thio-nucleotide triphosphates for random radical source introduction and on-demand backbone scission at co-introduced phosphorothioates.
source: Unfortunately, the original protocol (renamed 'MOHCA-gel' herein) required specially synthesized 2′-NH2-2′-deoxy-α-thio-nucleotide triphosphates for random radical source introduction and on-demand backbone scission at co-introduced phosphorothioates; a customized two-dimensional gel electrophoresis setup; radioactive labeling for the readout; and multiple experiments with both 5′ and 3′ end-labeling to achieve reasonable signal-to-noise (Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the prior MOHCA-gel method as reported in cited literature.

claim: The original MOHCA-gel protocol required a customized two-dimensional gel electrophoresis setup and radioactive labeling for the readout.
source: Unfortunately, the original protocol (renamed 'MOHCA-gel' herein) required specially synthesized 2′-NH2-2′-deoxy-α-thio-nucleotide triphosphates for random radical source introduction and on-demand backbone scission at co-introduced phosphorothioates; a customized two-dimensional gel electrophoresis setup; radioactive labeling for the readout; and multiple experiments with both 5′ and 3′ end-labeling to achieve reasonable signal-to-noise (Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the prior MOHCA-gel method as reported in cited literature.

claim: The limitations of MOHCA-gel prevented it from entering routine use or being tested along with M2 in RNA-puzzles trials.
source: These factors prevented MOHCA-gel from entering routine use or being tested along with M2 in RNA-puzzles trials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the practical limitations of the prior method and the history of RNA-puzzles.

claim: The MOHCA-seq workflow was designed to read out proximal nucleotide pairs by introducing radical sources at random locations into the RNA, creating radicals that initiate strand breaks at positions close in three dimensions to each source, and mapping the sequence positions of each strand break and its parent source.
source: The workflow was designed to read out proximal nucleotide pairs by introducing radical sources at random locations into the RNA, creating radicals that initiate strand breaks at positions close in three dimensions to each source, and mapping the sequence positions of each strand break and its parent source.
evidence: This describes the design and methodology of MOHCA-seq developed in this work.

claim: 2′-NH2-2′-dATP was randomly incorporated during transcription so that each RNA contained on average one or fewer modifications.
source: We randomly incorporated 2′-NH2-2′-dATP during transcription so that each RNA contained on average one or fewer modifications and then coupled these sites to isothiocyanobenzyl-Fe(III)•EDTA.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in MOHCA-seq.

claim: The reagents 2′-NH2-2′-dATP and isothiocyanobenzyl-Fe(III)•EDTA are commercially available.
source: We chose these reagents because they are commercially available and therefore can be readily acquired by other laboratories.
evidence: This is a factual statement about reagent availability.

claim: RNAs were folded in buffer containing 50 mM Na-HEPES pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, and any ligands appropriate for the system.
source: These RNAs were purified and then folded in buffer containing 50 mM Na-HEPES pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, and any ligands appropriate for the system (see below and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in MOHCA-seq.

claim: After folding, RNAs were fragmented by activating the Fenton reaction at the backbone-tethered Fe(III) atoms using ascorbate as a reducing agent.
source: After folding, RNAs were fragmented by activating the Fenton reaction at the backbone-tethered Fe(III) atoms using ascorbate as a reducing agent (Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for MOHCA-seq, with citation to prior work.

claim: MOHCA-seq simplifies and accelerates the readout using techniques developed for RNA-seq.
source: MOHCA-seq simplifies and accelerates the readout using techniques developed for RNA-seq (see, e.g., ref. [Ingolia et al., 2012]).
evidence: This describes the methodological advance of MOHCA-seq, with citation to RNA-seq techniques.

claim: The MOHCA-seq workflow includes an end-repair step using T4 polynucleotide kinase under conditions that promote its 3′-phosphatase activity.
source: To read out strand cleavage sites, the new workflow includes an end-repair step using T4 polynucleotide kinase under conditions that promote its 3′-phosphatase activity (Cameron and Uhlenbeck, 1977).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for MOHCA-seq, with citation to the enzymatic method.

claim: Reverse transcription was expected to stop at the nucleotide tethered to the bulky radical source at its C2′ position.
source: We expected reverse transcription to then stop at the nucleotide tethered to the bulky radical source at its C2′ position, providing a readout of the source position that is more convenient than the MOHCA-gel strand-scission method (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This describes the expected behavior based on the experimental design.

claim: Additional stop sites beyond radical source attachment positions were found, suggesting that reverse transcription could also terminate at sites of additional oxidative damage events.
source: However, we were surprised to find additional stop sites beyond these source attachment positions (Figure 2A, right), suggesting that reverse transcription could also terminate at sites of additional oxidative damage events, including not only radical-induced strand scission but also other products of ribose or nucleobase oxidation (e.g., 8-oxo-purines and 5-hydroxy-pyrimidines) (Yanagawa et al., 1990, 1992; Rhee et al., 1995; Pogozelski and Tullius, 1998; Barciszewski et al., 1999; Gong et al., 2006), which are indistinguishable at the cDNA level from stops at tethered radical sources.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to literature on oxidative damage.

claim: The high rate of reverse transcription stops would have been difficult to quantify in prior gel and capillary electrophoresis (CE) measurements.
source: This high rate of stops would have been difficult to quantify in prior gel and capillary electrophoresis (CE) measurements (Mitra et al., 2008; Kladwang et al., 2014); the rate and proximity of these stops to the radical source were confirmed through both CE and next-generation sequencing tests on a model hairpin RNA with a single radical source attachment position (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CE and sequencing shown in Figure 2, with citations to prior methods.

claim: The rate of reverse transcription-terminating oxidative damage events exceeds that of strand scission alone by many fold.
source: The rate of reverse transcription-terminating oxidative damage events exceeds that of strand scission alone by many fold (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MOHCA-seq enables detection of correlated events previously invisible to MOHCA-gel.
source: Thus, MOHCA-seq enables detection of correlated events previously invisible to MOHCA-gel, and we hypothesized that this significantly larger number of pairwise proximities would permit rapid ncRNA modeling with comparable accuracy to the prior method (Figure 2A,F–G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of MOHCA-seq and MOHCA-gel data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: MOHCA-seq does not require specially synthesized nucleotides or 2D gel electrophoresis.
source: Unlike MOHCA-gel, MOHCA-seq does not require specially synthesized nucleotides or 2D gel electrophoresis; the high-throughput sequencing readout improves the signal-to-noise as well as the length windows visible per experiment; and the detection of previously invisible oxidation events enhances the mapping coverage of a single experiment.
evidence: This describes the methodological advantages of MOHCA-seq over MOHCA-gel.

claim: The high-throughput sequencing readout improves the signal-to-noise as well as the length windows visible per experiment.
source: Unlike MOHCA-gel, MOHCA-seq does not require specially synthesized nucleotides or 2D gel electrophoresis; the high-throughput sequencing readout improves the signal-to-noise as well as the length windows visible per experiment; and the detection of previously invisible oxidation events enhances the mapping coverage of a single experiment.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of MOHCA-seq and MOHCA-gel data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The protocol's throughput is enhanced by its highly parallel nature, which was leveraged to co-load libraries for multiple RNAs on single sequencing runs.
source: The protocol's throughput is also enhanced by its highly parallel nature, which we leveraged to co-load libraries for multiple RNAs on single sequencing runs ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Raw sequencing counts from a single MOHCA-seq experiment exhibited dozens of pairwise proximity 'hits' throughout the P4-P6 ncRNA.
source: In comparison to prior MOHCA-gel data in which a single experiment yielded a few proximity pairs, raw sequencing counts from a single MOHCA-seq experiment exhibited dozens of pairwise proximity 'hits' throughout the ncRNA (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2F-G comparing MOHCA-seq and MOHCA-gel.

claim: The digital form of MOHCA-seq data enabled computational analysis to resolve further features through closure-based •OH correlation analysis (COHCOA).
source: Additionally, the digital form of MOHCA-seq data enabled computational analysis to resolve further features. Our analysis, called closure-based •OH correlation analysis (COHCOA), is described fully in the 'Materials and methods'.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis method developed for MOHCA-seq data.

claim: COHCOA assumes a two-dimensional background in the raw aligned sequencing data, which arises from two one-dimensional background profiles that are uncorrelated with tethered radical sources.
source: Briefly, COHCOA assumes a two-dimensional background in the raw aligned sequencing data, which arises from two one-dimensional background profiles that are uncorrelated with tethered radical sources: a strand scission profile (leading to horizontal striations) and a reverse transcription-terminating profile (leading to vertical striations) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the computational model underlying COHCOA analysis.

claim: COHCOA iteratively calculates and subtracts the two-dimensional background from observed data and corrects for reverse transcription attenuation.
source: Through iterative fitting, COHCOA calculates this two-dimensional background and subtracts it from the raw data and additionally corrects for reverse transcription attenuation.
evidence: This describes the computational procedure of COHCOA.

claim: COHCOA isolates the MOHCA-seq signal, which arises from oxidative damage that is spatially correlated with tethered radical sources.
source: The procedure isolates the MOHCA-seq signal, which arises from oxidative damage that is spatially correlated with tethered radical sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the output of COHCOA analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The P4–P6 RNA has five major helical secondary structure elements: P4, P5a, P5b, P5c, and P6.
source: The P4–P6 RNA has five major helical secondary structure elements, P4, P5a, P5b, P5c, and P6, which were originally characterized at high resolution by crystallography and recently confirmed to occur in solution at base-pair resolution by M2 experiments (Kladwang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and M2 experiments cited in the text.

claim: MOHCA-seq proximity hits corresponded to radicals diffusing across the major and minor grooves of P4-P6 helices.
source: Indeed, MOHCA-seq proximity hits corresponded to radicals diffusing across the major and minor grooves of each of these helices (visible as two separate branches, arrows in Figure 1D), confirming the M2 secondary structure, albeit at lower resolution (compare Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 1D and comparison to M2 data in Figure 1C.

claim: Nearly two dozen tertiary proximities appeared as punctate hits in P4-P6 MOHCA-seq data, including features marking the bend at the J5/5a hinge, the A-minor contact between the A-rich bulge and P4, and the docking of the L5b tetraloop into the J6a/6b receptor.
source: Importantly, nearly two dozen tertiary proximities, including features marking the bend at the J5/5a hinge, the A-minor contact between the A-rich bulge and P4, and the docking of the L5b tetraloop into the J6a/6b receptor, appeared as punctate hits (Figure 1D–F); only the last of these was clearly observed in M2 mapping (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: MOHCA-seq features appeared at similar positions (but with variable intensities) whether radical sources were attached at A, C, G, or U.
source: We observed MOHCA-seq features at similar positions (but with variable intensities) whether radical sources were attached at A, C, G, or U (Figure 2H–K); whether the ratio of 2′-NH2-modified nucleotides to standard nucleotides was 1:5, 1:2, or 5:4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); or whether the fragmentation reaction time was 5, 10, or 30 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H-K and supplementary figures.

claim: Even after 30 min of radical source activation, the proximity information in the experimental data remains clearly visible without noticeable increase in background.
source: In particular, even after 30 min of radical source activation, the proximity information in the experimental data remains clearly visible without noticeable increase in background, suggesting that the radical source cleaves itself off the RNA in minutes, limiting the reaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and CE analysis.

claim: The radical source cleaves itself off the RNA in minutes, limiting the reaction.
source: In particular, even after 30 min of radical source activation, the proximity information in the experimental data remains clearly visible without noticeable increase in background, suggesting that the radical source cleaves itself off the RNA in minutes, limiting the reaction. CE of ascorbate-treated end-labeled RNA supported this mechanism of self-limiting the reaction (see also Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by experimental data and cited prior work.

claim: A few weak signals in the proximity maps that were not predicted by the crystal structure may be caused by perturbations of the ncRNA structure by radical source attachment or by conformational dynamics of the RNA or the ∼11 Å benzyl-thiourea linker.
source: A few weak signals in the proximity maps that were not predicted by the crystal structure (pink circles, Figure 1D) may be caused by perturbations of the ncRNA structure by radical source attachment or by conformational dynamics of the RNA or the ∼11 Å benzyl-thiourea linker tethering the radical source to the RNA backbone.
evidence: This is speculation about the origin of unexplained signals in the data.

claim: MOHCA-seq data enabled 3D computational modeling of the P4–P6 domain to helical resolution or better without crystallographic information.
source: Based on previous MOHCA-gel studies, we expected that our MOHCA-seq data would enable 3D computational modeling of the P4–P6 domain to helical resolution or better without crystallographic information.
evidence: This expectation is based on prior MOHCA-gel work and is validated by the modeling results presented.

claim: The FARNA with full-atom refinement algorithm in Rosetta was used for modeling.
source: We used the FARNA with full-atom refinement algorithm in Rosetta (Das et al., 2010) for modeling, described in detail in the 'Materials and methods'.
evidence: This describes the computational method used, with citation to prior work.

claim: Helices were pre-assembled in Rosetta to reduce the computational expense of sampling helices, which primarily adopt A-form conformations.
source: First, to reduce the computational expense of sampling helices, which primarily adopt A-form conformations, we pre-assembled secondary structure elements in Rosetta.
evidence: This describes the computational strategy used in modeling.

claim: Helices derived from M2 and 1D SHAPE mapping were used for modeling to mimic the lack of high-resolution data for cases of blind RNA structure prediction.
source: To mimic the lack of high-resolution data for cases of blind RNA structure prediction, we used helices derived from M2 and 1D SHAPE mapping for modeling.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach designed to simulate blind prediction conditions.

claim: Global modeling in Rosetta was performed in two stages: generating an initial set of over 10,000 low-resolution models using FARNA, then minimizing the 1/6 of the models with the lowest Rosetta energy score using full-atom refinement.
source: Second, we performed global modeling in Rosetta in two stages. We generated an initial set of over 10,000 low-resolution models using FARNA in parallel, independent modeling runs; then, we minimized the 1/6 of the models with the lowest Rosetta energy score using full-atom refinement.
evidence: This describes the computational modeling protocol used.

claim: MOHCA-seq data were included to constrain sampling in both stages of Rosetta modeling.
source: In both stages, we included MOHCA-seq data to constrain sampling.
evidence: This describes how MOHCA-seq data were used in the modeling.

claim: A list of pairs of residues suggested to be proximal by MOHCA-seq data was generated by identifying peaks that were distinguishable from the local background signal and not attributable to secondary structure.
source: To apply the MOHCA-seq data in Rosetta, we generated a list of pairs of residues that were suggested to be proximal by the data by identifying peaks that were (1) distinguishable from the local background signal and (2) not attributable to secondary structure, based on secondary structures inferred by M2 (Kladwang et al., 2011a) (purple and pink circles, Figure 1D and tabulated in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the procedure for selecting MOHCA-seq constraints for modeling.

claim: All MOHCA-seq data were used in modeling, including weak features not explained by the crystal structure, anticipating that the modeling would automatically determine the maximal subset of contacts consistent with each other and with a single structure.
source: As in prior work (Das et al., 2008), we assumed that signals due to dynamic heterogeneity would be weak compared to those due to stable tertiary proximities. Therefore, we used all data, including the few weak features not explained by the crystal structure (pink circles, Figure 1D), anticipating that the modeling would automatically determine the maximal subset of contacts consistent with each other and with a single structure.
evidence: This describes the modeling strategy and assumptions, with citation to prior work.

claim: Conformational sampling in Rosetta was constrained by applying a smooth pseudo-energy potential between each pair of residues in the list that favored conformations with the residues between 0 and 30 Å apart.
source: Conformational sampling in Rosetta was constrained by applying a smooth pseudo-energy potential (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) between each pair of residues in the list that favored conformations with the residues between 0 and 30 Å apart and disfavored conformations with the residues more than 30 Å apart.
evidence: This describes the computational constraint function used in modeling.

claim: The pseudo-energy potential used for MOHCA-seq constraints was similar to that developed previously for MOHCA-gel analysis.
source: This potential, which was similar to that developed previously for MOHCA-gel analysis, was suggested based on observed correlation of the MOHCA-seq intensity to distances in residue pairs involved in secondary structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and ref. [Das et al., 2008]) and was validated below.
evidence: This describes the basis for the constraint potential, with citation to prior work and reference to validation data.

claim: A single representative model was selected by clustering the lowest-energy 3% of the refined models using Rosetta.
source: Finally, we selected a single representative model by clustering the lowest-energy 3% of the refined models using Rosetta.
evidence: This describes the model selection procedure.

claim: The final single model of the MCM pipeline is the model with the largest number of neighboring models within the RMSD threshold, called the 'cluster center'.
source: As in protein structure modeling (Shortle et al., 1998), the final single model of this MCM pipeline is the model with the largest number of neighboring models within the RMSD threshold, called the 'cluster center', which is not necessarily the model with the lowest Rosetta energy score.
evidence: This describes the model selection criterion, with citation to analogous protein modeling approaches.

claim: The cluster center represents the best tertiary structure prediction of the MCM pipeline for automated Rosetta modeling guided by experimental data.
source: The cluster center represents the best tertiary structure prediction of the MCM pipeline for automated Rosetta modeling guided by experimental data.
evidence: This defines the interpretation of the cluster center model.

claim: The RMSD threshold used for clustering represents the intra-cluster RMSD between models in the cluster and is used to calculate an in situ RMSD estimate, representing the precision of modeling.
source: The RMSD threshold used for clustering represents the intra-cluster RMSD between models in the cluster and is used to calculate an in situ RMSD estimate, representing the precision of modeling (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes how precision is estimated from the modeling.

claim: The accuracy of the MCM model was calculated as the all-heavy-atom RMSD between the cluster center and the crystal structure.
source: The accuracy of the MCM model was calculated as the all-heavy-atom RMSD between the cluster center and the crystal structure, as in our previous study (Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes how accuracy is calculated, with citation to prior work.

claim: The cluster center of the MCM pipeline for P4-P6 had an accuracy of 8.6 Å RMSD to the crystal structure.
source: For the P4–P6 benchmark case, we found that the cluster center of the MCM pipeline had an accuracy of 8.6 Å RMSD to the crystal structure (Figures 1F, 3A and Table 1), which was within the 16.5 Å precision of the modeling estimated from the clustering threshold (Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figures 1F, 3A and Table 1.

claim: The 8.6 Å accuracy of the P4-P6 cluster center was within the 16.5 Å precision of the modeling estimated from the clustering threshold.
source: For the P4–P6 benchmark case, we found that the cluster center of the MCM pipeline had an accuracy of 8.6 Å RMSD to the crystal structure (Figures 1F, 3A and Table 1), which was within the 16.5 Å precision of the modeling estimated from the clustering threshold (Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Table 2.

claim: MCM is capable of defining the global 3D structure of RNA at near the resolution of a single-nucleotide register shift (6 Å) even when weak MOHCA-seq features not explained by the crystal structure are used to constrain modeling.
source: This suggests that MCM is capable of defining the global 3D structure of the RNA, without crystallographic information, at near the resolution of a single-nucleotide register shift (6 Å) even when weak MOHCA-seq features not explained by the crystal structure are used to constrain modeling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the P4-P6 modeling results.

claim: Performing Rosetta modeling without MOHCA-seq pairwise constraints led to a model with 38.3 Å accuracy to the crystal structure for P4-P6.
source: Performing the same Rosetta modeling protocol without MOHCA-seq pairwise constraints led to a strikingly worse model with 38.3 Å accuracy to the crystal structure (Figure 3A and Table 1), demonstrating that MOHCA-seq constraints are required for accurate modeling.
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3A and Table 1.

claim: MOHCA-seq constraints are required for accurate modeling.
source: Performing the same Rosetta modeling protocol without MOHCA-seq pairwise constraints led to a strikingly worse model with 38.3 Å accuracy to the crystal structure (Figure 3A and Table 1), demonstrating that MOHCA-seq constraints are required for accurate modeling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of modeling with and without MOHCA-seq constraints.

claim: The 8.6 Å accuracy of the P4-P6 cluster center was better than the previous 13 Å accuracy of modeling guided by MOHCA-gel data.
source: The 8.6 Å accuracy of the cluster center was better than the previous 13 Å accuracy of modeling guided by MOHCA-gel data, which were collected at substantially greater experimental expense and did not allow base-pair resolution inference of secondary structure, as is now provided by M2 analysis (Das et al., 2008).
evidence: This comparison is supported by the current results and citation to prior MOHCA-gel work.

claim: MCM achieved 7.6 Å accuracy for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer.
source: Indeed, this resolution was attained by MCM in all cases: 7.6 Å for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer; 7.9 Å for the glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain; 11.9 Å for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer (compare to RNA-puzzle 6 models, Figure 3—figure supplement 4); and 11.1 Å (ribozyme) and 14.5 Å (ribozyme including substrate) for the class I ligase (Shechner et al., 2009) (Figure 3B–E and Table 1; clusters with knots were not accepted, see Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: MCM achieved 7.9 Å accuracy for the glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain.
source: Indeed, this resolution was attained by MCM in all cases: 7.6 Å for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer; 7.9 Å for the glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain; 11.9 Å for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer (compare to RNA-puzzle 6 models, Figure 3—figure supplement 4); and 11.1 Å (ribozyme) and 14.5 Å (ribozyme including substrate) for the class I ligase (Shechner et al., 2009) (Figure 3B–E and Table 1; clusters with knots were not accepted, see Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: MCM achieved 11.9 Å accuracy for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer.
source: Indeed, this resolution was attained by MCM in all cases: 7.6 Å for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer; 7.9 Å for the glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain; 11.9 Å for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer (compare to RNA-puzzle 6 models, Figure 3—figure supplement 4); and 11.1 Å (ribozyme) and 14.5 Å (ribozyme including substrate) for the class I ligase (Shechner et al., 2009) (Figure 3B–E and Table 1; clusters with knots were not accepted, see Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3D and Table 1.

claim: MCM achieved 11.1 Å accuracy for the class I ligase ribozyme core and 14.5 Å accuracy for the ribozyme including substrate.
source: Indeed, this resolution was attained by MCM in all cases: 7.6 Å for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer; 7.9 Å for the glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain; 11.9 Å for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer (compare to RNA-puzzle 6 models, Figure 3—figure supplement 4); and 11.1 Å (ribozyme) and 14.5 Å (ribozyme including substrate) for the class I ligase (Shechner et al., 2009) (Figure 3B–E and Table 1; clusters with knots were not accepted, see Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3E and Table 1.

claim: The lack of correlation between the fraction of satisfied MOHCA-seq pairwise constraints and the accuracy of the models suggests that unsatisfied constraints are due to conformational fluctuations in the RNA or radical-source linkers around the dominant global structures.
source: The lack of correlation between the fraction of satisfied MOHCA-seq pairwise constraints and the accuracy of the models (Table 2) suggests that unsatisfied constraints are due to conformational fluctuations in the RNA or radical-source linkers around the dominant global structures of these molecules, rather than systematic structural shifts or incomplete computational sampling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from analysis of constraint satisfaction data in Table 2.

claim: Highly sampled computational modeling is able to filter out inconsistent constraints, as has been observed in prior macromolecule modeling based on pairwise information.
source: The generally consistent accuracy of these predictions supports our hypothesis that highly sampled computational modeling is able to filter out such inconsistent constraints, as has been observed in prior macromolecule modeling based on pairwise information (Bowers et al., 2000; Das et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and citations to prior work on constraint-based modeling.

claim: The relationship of MOHCA-seq signal intensities to pairwise distances seen in crystal structures was recovered by MCM models.
source: Further supporting the assumptions of modeling, including the form of the pseudo-energy function, the relationship of MOHCA-seq signal intensities to pairwise distances seen in crystal structures was recovered by MCM models (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: M2/Rosetta modeling without MOHCA-seq constraints produced dramatically less accurate models for all tested ncRNA domains.
source: Again, we tested the necessity of MOHCA-seq data for completing the MCM pipeline by performing identical modeling of all ncRNA domains without MOHCA-seq constraints (M2/Rosetta modeling). Just as for the P4–P6 domain, these runs produced dramatically less accurate models, as can be visually assessed (Figure 3) and quantitated by both RMSD to the crystal structure and statistical significance (Hajdin et al., 2010) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of modeling results with and without MOHCA-seq shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: M2 data correctly discriminated between literature models of the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer's secondary structure.
source: For this RNA-puzzle target, we previously collected and disseminated M2 data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) that correctly discriminated between literature models of this ncRNA's secondary structure (Peselis & Serganov, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by M2 data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to the crystal structure.

claim: M2 data for the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer did not disambiguate between a range of 3D structures, with ten submitted models giving RMSDs from 12.1 Å to 32.8 Å to the crystal structure.
source: However, these data did not disambiguate between a range of 3D structures, and our ten submitted models gave RMSDs from 12.1 Å to 32.8 Å to the subsequently released riboswitch aptamer crystal structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-puzzle submission results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The full MCM pipeline resolved tertiary contacts between the peripheral and core regions of the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer.
source: Indeed, the full MCM pipeline resolved tertiary contacts between the peripheral and core regions of the ncRNA (Figure 3D), and automated modeling converged to a structure defined with 13.9 Å resolution (in situ precision estimate), which achieved 11.9 Å RMSD to the crystal structure (Figure 3D, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and 'Materials and methods'), comparable to the accuracy of our best RNA-puzzle submission and clearly defining the global structure to helix resolution.
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq data and modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: MCM modeling of the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer converged to a structure defined with 13.9 Å resolution (in situ precision estimate), which achieved 11.9 Å RMSD to the crystal structure.
source: Indeed, the full MCM pipeline resolved tertiary contacts between the peripheral and core regions of the ncRNA (Figure 3D), and automated modeling converged to a structure defined with 13.9 Å resolution (in situ precision estimate), which achieved 11.9 Å RMSD to the crystal structure (Figure 3D, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and 'Materials and methods'), comparable to the accuracy of our best RNA-puzzle submission and clearly defining the global structure to helix resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3D and Table 1.

claim: M2 data for the lariat-capping ribozyme supported literature models of the ncRNA's secondary structure and suggested two additional tertiary contacts creating a 'ring' around the ribozyme.
source: As part of this blind challenge, we previously collected and shared M2 data (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) that supported literature models of the ncRNA's secondary structure and suggested two additional tertiary contacts creating a 'ring' around the ribozyme.
evidence: This is supported by M2 data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: MOHCA-seq data for the lariat-capping ribozyme highlighted potential errors in extended peripheral regions P2.1 and P4–P6.
source: After developing MOHCA-seq but before the release of the lariat-capping ribozyme crystal structure, we completed the MCM pipeline by acquiring MOHCA-seq data for the ncRNA (Figure 3F), and the resulting map highlighted potential errors in these extended peripheral regions.
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Blind refinement of the lariat-capping ribozyme peripheral regions based on full MCM data improved accuracy from an original RMSD of 17.0 Å to a final RMSD of 11.2 Å.
source: We then blindly refined the peripheral regions based on the full MCM data (Figure 3F and Table 1), and the subsequent release of the ribozyme crystal structure (Meyer et al., 2014) confirmed that their accuracy significantly improved, from an original RMSD of 17.0 Å (original RNA-puzzle submission, M2/Rosetta) to a final RMSD of 11.2 Å (full MCM, i.e., M2/MOHCA-seq/Rosetta).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of modeling results before and after MCM refinement, shown in Figure 3F and Table 1.

claim: The global accuracy of lariat-capping ribozyme models improved to a range of RMSDs from 7.6 to 8.9 Å over the full ribozyme, compared to the original submission with 9.6 Å overall RMSD.
source: The global accuracy of the models also improved, with a range of RMSDs over the full ribozyme from 7.6 to 8.9 Å, compared to our original submission, which turned out to have an overall RMSD accuracy of 9.6 Å.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: The full MCM pipeline demonstrated the ability to detect errors and to consistently and blindly refine ncRNA structures to 1-nm resolution or better throughout complex structures.
source: Taken together, these results rigorously demonstrated the ability of the full MCM pipeline to detect errors and to consistently and blindly refine ncRNA structures to 1-nm resolution or better throughout complex structures.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the benchmark and blind test results presented.

claim: Understanding riboswitch structures in the absence of ligands is critical for dissecting mechanisms of ligand capture and modulation of gene expression.
source: Riboswitches form a major class of ncRNAs, and understanding their structures in the absence of ligands is critical for dissecting mechanisms of ligand capture and modulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Crystal structures and solution scattering of a few ligand-free riboswitch aptamers have suggested the possibility of extensive preformed tertiary structure in special cases.
source: While crystal structures and solution scattering of a few ligand-free riboswitch aptamers have suggested the possibility of extensive preformed tertiary structure in special cases (Serganov et al., 2008; Baird et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2012), whether these structures are generally sampled in solution in the absence of ligand has remained poorly understood due to the lack of an unbiased, high-throughput solution structural technique.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Whether preformed tertiary structures are generally sampled in solution in the absence of ligand has remained poorly understood due to the lack of an unbiased, high-throughput solution structural technique.
source: While crystal structures and solution scattering of a few ligand-free riboswitch aptamers have suggested the possibility of extensive preformed tertiary structure in special cases (Serganov et al., 2008; Baird et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2012), whether these structures are generally sampled in solution in the absence of ligand has remained poorly understood due to the lack of an unbiased, high-throughput solution structural technique.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field and the gap that MCM addresses.

claim: The computational modeling of heterogeneous conformational ensembles from experimental data is an open problem.
source: Because the computational modeling of heterogeneous conformational ensembles from experimental data is an open problem (Beauchamp et al., 2014; Salmon et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2014), our primary conclusions below are based on the M2 and MOHCA-seq data themselves, with Rosetta modeling carried out for initial visualization only (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on ensemble modeling.

claim: Prior studies on the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer revealed an extended conformation transiently interconverting with a 'docked' conformation that shares at least one tertiary contact with the ligand-bound docked state (P1b/P2 tetraloop/receptor).
source: We first applied MCM to the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer without its ligand, which had been previously studied with state-of-the-art small-angle X-ray scattering, single-molecule FRET, and kinetic analysis (Kulshina et al., 2009; Wood et al., 2012). These prior studies revealed an extended conformation of this ncRNA transiently interconverting with a 'docked' conformation that shares at least one tertiary contact with the ligand-bound docked state (P1b/P2 tetraloop/receptor).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biophysical studies.

claim: M2 measurements gave P1a, P1b, and P2 helices in both ligand-free and ligand-bound states of the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer.
source: In terms of secondary structure, M2 measurements gave P1a, P1b, and P2 helices in both ligand-free and ligand-bound states, up to possible rearrangements in edge base pairs (Kladwang et al., 2011a), and MOHCA-seq additionally confirmed all 3 helices in both states (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by M2 data cited and MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MOHCA-seq confirmed all 3 helices (P1a, P1b, P2) in both ligand-free and ligand-bound states of the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer.
source: In terms of secondary structure, M2 measurements gave P1a, P1b, and P2 helices in both ligand-free and ligand-bound states, up to possible rearrangements in edge base pairs (Kladwang et al., 2011a), and MOHCA-seq additionally confirmed all 3 helices in both states (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Unambiguous proximities between several segments of P1b and P2 detected in the ligand-bound state of the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer were also observed at the same locations, albeit weakly, in the ligand-free state.
source: In terms of tertiary structure, unambiguous proximities between several segments of P1b and P2 that were detected in the ligand-bound state (Figure 4A, left) were also observed at the same locations, albeit weakly, in the ligand-free state (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Tertiary features in the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer disappeared in solution conditions without Mg2+.
source: To test that these tertiary features were not due to noise or experimental artifacts in MOHCA-seq experiments or data processing, we confirmed that they disappeared in solution conditions without Mg2+ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by control MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The matching 'fingerprints' of cross-helix tertiary features in ligand-free and ligand-bound MOHCA-seq maps provided evidence that the ligand-free c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer samples the same tertiary conformation as the ligand-bound docked state at nanometer resolution.
source: The matching 'fingerprints' of cross-helix tertiary features in ligand-free and ligand-bound MOHCA-seq maps provided evidence that the ligand-free riboswitch aptamer samples the same tertiary conformation as the ligand-bound docked state at nanometer resolution, including and going beyond the known tetraloop/receptor contact.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of MOHCA-seq data in different conditions.

claim: The conformational heterogeneity of the top cluster for the ligand-free c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer was significantly larger than clustering of ligand-bound states (9.8 Å vs 6.8 Å).
source: To visualize the ensemble, we performed Rosetta modeling as above and discovered that the conformational heterogeneity of the top cluster was significantly larger than clustering of ligand-bound states above (9.8 Å vs 6.8 Å, respectively; Table 2), suggesting that a significant fraction of the visible variance (Figure 4C) arises from actual RNA conformational dynamics rather than from modeling uncertainties.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Table 2 and Figure 4C.

claim: Four of the five lowest energy models for the ligand-free c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer were primarily extended and without tertiary contacts, with one showing a more compact state similar to the one stabilized by ligand.
source: As in NMR studies of dynamic molecules, we therefore inspected an ensemble of models with the lowest Rosetta energy score instead of focusing on the cluster center; the resulting ensemble was used for initial visualization only (Al-Hashimi, 2007; Bothe et al., 2011; Salmon et al., 2014). Four of the five lowest energy models were primarily extended and without tertiary contacts, with one showing a more compact state similar to the one stabilized by ligand.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MOHCA-seq data are consistent with a picture of the ligand-free state of the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer primarily adopting extended conformations but also interconverting to more compact ones.
source: The MOHCA-seq data are thus consistent with a picture of the ligand-free state of the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer primarily adopting extended conformations but also interconverting to more compact ones (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from MOHCA-seq data and modeling results.

claim: The glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain consists of two glycine-binding aptamers connected by a linker.
source: The glycine riboswitch ligand-binding domain consists of two glycine-binding aptamers connected by a linker; the formation of cross-aptamer contacts upon ligand binding could explain the cooperativity of glycine binding between the aptamers (Erion and Strobel, 2011; Kladwang et al., 2012a; Esquiaqui et al., 2014; Ruff and Strobel, 2014), but has not been directly visualized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on the glycine riboswitch.

claim: Previous M2 data indicated that three major helical elements P1, P2, and P3 were formed by each of the two glycine riboswitch aptamers, both with and without glycine.
source: In terms of secondary structure, previous M2 data indicated that three major helical elements P1, P2, and P3 were formed by each of the two aptamers, both with and without glycine (Kladwang et al., 2011a); MOHCA-seq data gave additional support for this six-helix secondary structure being preformed without ligand (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cited M2 data and MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MOHCA-seq data gave additional support for the six-helix secondary structure of the glycine riboswitch being preformed without ligand.
source: In terms of secondary structure, previous M2 data indicated that three major helical elements P1, P2, and P3 were formed by each of the two aptamers, both with and without glycine (Kladwang et al., 2011a); MOHCA-seq data gave additional support for this six-helix secondary structure being preformed without ligand (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tertiary proximity hits observed both within and across the two glycine riboswitch aptamers in the glycine-bound state were retained, though weakened, in the absence of glycine.
source: Strikingly, tertiary proximity hits observed both within and across the two aptamers in the glycine-bound state were retained, though weakened, in the absence of glycine (Figure 5A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3H.

claim: Tertiary proximities in the glycine riboswitch were not detectable in conditions without Mg2+.
source: Analogous to our control experiments for the c-di-GMP riboswitch aptamer, these tertiary proximities were not detectable in conditions without Mg2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly supported by control MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Rosetta modeling of the ligand-free glycine riboswitch gave a structural ensemble with an approximately similar global structure but substantially more conformational variance than the ligand-bound state.
source: Completing the MCM pipeline, Rosetta modeling of the ligand-free state with M2/MOHCA-seq constraints gave a structural ensemble with an approximately similar global structure but substantially more conformational variance than the ligand-bound state (Figure 5C and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5C and Table 2.

claim: The preformed tertiary proximities detected by MCM in the ligand-free glycine riboswitch aptamer depend critically on a leader sequence that stabilizes a K-turn linker between the aptamers.
source: As an example, we discovered that the preformed tertiary proximities detected by MCM in the ligand-free riboswitch aptamer depend critically on at least one junction element, a leader sequence that was missed in crystallographic studies but later shown to stabilize a K-turn linker between the aptamers (Figure 5D,E) (Kladwang et al., 2012a; Esquiaqui et al., 2014; Ruff and Strobel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq data comparing constructs with and without the leader sequence, shown in Figure 5D,E, and citations to prior work.

claim: Long-standing controversies in modeling the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer raised the possibility of differences in both secondary and tertiary structure in states with and without ligand.
source: Compared to the riboswitch aptamers above, much less was previously known about the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer. Indeed, long-standing controversies in modeling this ncRNA raised the possibility of differences in both secondary and tertiary structure in states with and without ligand (Ravnum and Andersson, 2001; Nahvi et al., 2002; Vitreschak et al., 2003; Nahvi et al., 2004; Barrick and Breaker, 2007; Miao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on the AdoCbl riboswitch.

claim: MCM revealed striking similarities between ligand-bound and ligand-free states of the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer, most clearly visible in MOHCA-seq data.
source: Nevertheless, MCM revealed striking similarities between the states, most clearly visible in MOHCA-seq data (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Features for six major helical stacks in the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer appeared identical with and without ligand.
source: In terms of secondary structure, features for six major helical stacks appeared identical with and without ligand.
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MOHCA-seq data without ligand showed reduction but not complete loss of strong tertiary proximities between helices that enclose the ligand-binding site in the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer.
source: In terms of tertiary structure, the data without ligand showed reduction but not complete loss of strong tertiary proximities between helices that enclose the ligand-binding site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rosetta modeling of the ligand-free AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer produced an initial visualization of a loose structural ensemble that samples, but does not stably remain in, the ligand-bound structure within the nanometer resolution of the MOHCA-seq method.
source: As above, Rosetta modeling produced an initial visualization of a loose structural ensemble that samples, but does not stably remain in, the ligand-bound structure within the nanometer resolution of the MOHCA-seq method (Figure 6B and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6B and Table 2.

claim: The sole long-range tertiary interaction in the AdoCbl-binding site (an A-minor contact between J11-10 and helix P6) was necessary for ligand binding but not the global tertiary proximities measured by MOHCA-seq.
source: As a first example, we found that the sole long-range tertiary interaction in the AdoCbl-binding site (an A-minor contact between J11-10 and helix P6) was necessary for ligand binding but not the global tertiary proximities measured by MOHCA-seq (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by MOHCA-seq and 1D chemical mapping data on the A124U/A125U mutant shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The ligand-free proximities in the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer arise not from direct tertiary contacts but from conformational preferences encoded in the riboswitch aptamer junctions.
source: Like the data for the glycine riboswitch aptamers above, these data further suggest that the ligand-free proximities in the AdoCbl riboswitch aptamer arise not from direct tertiary contacts but from conformational preferences encoded in the riboswitch aptamer junctions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutational analysis and MOHCA-seq data.

claim: The discovery of cellular internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements in the 5′-UTRs of the Hox mRNAs has suggested new roles of structured ncRNAs in mammalian development.
source: The discovery in recent months of cellular internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements in the 5′-UTRs of the Hox mRNAs has suggested new roles of structured ncRNAs in mammalian development (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The secondary structure of the HoxA9 IRES domain was determined by M2, along with in vivo mutation-rescue experiments that confirmed key helix elements.
source: The secondary structure of the domain was determined by M2, along with in vivo mutation-rescue experiments that confirmed key helix elements (Figure 7A) (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by M2 data shown in Figure 7A and citation to prior work.

claim: MOHCA-seq data corroborated the secondary structure of the HoxA9 IRES domain and provided independent support for a pseudoknot (pk3-4) connecting two arms of a four-way junction.
source: We collected MOHCA-seq data that corroborated the secondary structure described previously and provided independent support for a pseudoknot (pk3-4) connecting two arms of a four-way junction, a common feature of viral IRESes that has not been demonstrated for cellular IRESes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is directly supported by MOHCA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A pseudoknot is a common feature of viral IRESes that has not been demonstrated for cellular IRESes.
source: We collected MOHCA-seq data that corroborated the secondary structure described previously and provided independent support for a pseudoknot (pk3-4) connecting two arms of a four-way junction, a common feature of viral IRESes that has not been demonstrated for cellular IRESes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: MCM modeling revealed a core four-way junction aligned by the pseudoknot in the HoxA9 IRES domain, defined at an estimated resolution of 19.5 Å.
source: We completed the MCM pipeline to computationally model the domain's global 3D structure, revealing a core four-way junction aligned by the pseudoknot, defined at an estimated resolution of 19.5 Å, similar to the loose ensembles seen in our MCM models of ligand-free riboswitch aptamers (Figure 7C and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7C and Table 2.

claim: Modeling of the HoxA9 IRES domain that used an alternative pk3-4-free secondary structure gave a final conformation within 19.5 Å RMSD of the cluster center with pseudoknot.
source: Supporting this global structure and estimated resolution, modeling that used an alternative pk3-4-free secondary structure gave a final conformation within 19.5 Å RMSD of the cluster center with pseudoknot (Figure 7D; alternative secondary structure from Extended Data Figure 6C in ref. [Xue et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MCM appears to be the only front-line technique able to resolve the HoxA9 IRES domain's global structure in isolation, given the conformational heterogeneity of this 176-nucleotide ncRNA in the absence of partners.
source: Given the conformational heterogeneity of this 176-nucleotide ncRNA in the absence of partners, MCM appears to be the only front-line technique able to resolve this domain's global structure in isolation, which we propose to be a recognition site for the mammalian 80S ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the capabilities of MCM demonstrated in the study and the limitations of other techniques for heterogeneous systems.

claim: The HoxA9 IRES domain is proposed to be a recognition site for the mammalian 80S ribosome.
source: Given the conformational heterogeneity of this 176-nucleotide ncRNA in the absence of partners, MCM appears to be the only front-line technique able to resolve this domain's global structure in isolation, which we propose to be a recognition site for the mammalian 80S ribosome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the function of IRES elements.

claim: MCM models of the HoxA9 IRES domain provide fiducial landmarks to seek in upcoming cryo-electron microscopy studies of the HoxA9 IRES in the presence of the ribosome and other macromolecular partners.
source: These models provide fiducial landmarks to seek in upcoming cryo-electron microscopy studies of the HoxA9 IRES in the presence of the ribosome and other macromolecular partners (PDB-formatted models are available online in Source code 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the models for future studies.
